extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of English language, dialect, and literary history; educated general readership interested in philology and pronunciation
extracted.subtask_description: Close literary-historical analysis of American (Yankee) pronunciations, vocabulary, and usages, showing their antiquity, sources, and aesthetic evaluation. The page argues for the legitimacy of many dialectal forms by citing historical English literature and linguistic descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgarity is in thought, not in the word
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly speaking, vulgarity is in the thought, and not in the word or the way of pronouncing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial/prescriptive judgement: pronunciation or apparent 'vulgar' forms (e.g., Yankee pronunciations) are not inherently vulgar if the thought is not vulgar. Examples/contrast: Modern French may be 'barbarously vulgar' compared with Latin on etymological grounds, but lexical change alone does not imply moral or aesthetic vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent settles by ease and quickness of utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Accent will finally settle on the syllable dictated by greater ease and therefore quickness of utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains contemporary shifts (e.g., Amer'ican vs Ameri'can; blas'-phemous vs blasphem'ous). Use this principle to predict or evaluate where stress moves in evolving pronunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/poetic evidence legitimizes dialectal pronunciations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many so-called Yankee or rustic pronunciations have authority in older English literature and therefore are not mere corruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive citations: Chaucer, Spenser, Donne, Dryden, Milton, Beaumont & Fletcher, Coventry Plays, Paston Letters etc. Use rhymes and spellings in these sources as evidence when assessing legitimacy of a pronunciation (e.g., 'reule', 'noo', 'ferce', 'pairlous').

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention or revival of French (Gallic) sounds can explain dialectal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Preservation of French sounds in single letters and diphthongs accounts for certain Yankee pronunciations and spellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drop of u in -our endings (Howell); 'cowcumber' ~ 'concombre'; soft u in rule/truth; 'noo' possibly from nouveau/neuf. Use etymological ties to Norman/French to justify forms like 'ferce' for 'fierce' or 'pairlous' for 'perilous'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling, eye logic, and analogical influence shape pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual analogy and spelling-history (the 'logic of the eye') have affected both pronunciation and spelling—sometimes adding letters (e.g., l in could) or preserving them elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an 'l' foisted into 'could'; 'belcony' (Wren); influence of printed spellings on speech. When evaluating a form, consider orthographic history as a causal factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, sharp-cut enunciation is an aesthetic ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear and sharp-cut enunciation is one of the crowning charms and elegances of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's prescriptive preference: such enunciation likened to 'coins fresh from the mint' and contrasted with 'wet-fuse drawl.' But the author admits that elisions and older pronunciations can be praiseworthy in certain poetic or dialectal contexts (e.g., Allan Ramsay, Burns). Use this as an evaluative standard while allowing stylistic exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elision and dropping of final consonants can be stylistically acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The dropping of final consonants is not necessarily disagreeable; it appears in respected poets and old speech and may be acceptable depending on register and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Allan Ramsay, Burns, Chaucer, ballad-singers, and older spellings ('boun' for 'boon/ bound') as precedent. When judging speech, consider whether elision serves dialectal authenticity or poetic meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of double negatives may be regretted as loss of an older feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The double negative was once universal in English and its loss might be regretted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note rather than strict prescriptive rule: double negatives were common like in neo-Latin languages. Use this perspective when evaluating the 'correctness' of older versus modern usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymological logic can justify forms often labeled vulgar
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms criticized as vulgar (e.g., 'illy' as an adverb) have etymological or logical grounds and historical precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'illy' reflects that 'ill' was originally an adjective and 'illy' followed as an adverb; dictionaries may call it inferior class but etymology supports its existence. Use etymology to assess whether a form is a baseless corruption or an inherited pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most supposed Americanisms are borrowings rather than original inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few genuine American coinages; most alleged Americanisms are borrowings from French, German, Spanish, or Indian, or survivals of older English forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'bogus' probably from French bagasse; 'maiz' and 'canoa' borrowed; many items (fall for autumn, crick for creek, loan/lend forms) occur in older English. Evaluate claims of originality by searching historical attestations and foreign-source possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions, colloquialisms, and altered forms often appear in early English literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms like 'more 'n', 'gin' for 'given', 'colume' for 'column', 'stret along', 'right here' appear in early plays and writers and therefore are not modern corruptions per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literary examples (Chaucer, Gower, Warner, Middleton, Dryden, the Coventry and Chester plays, etc.) to justify colloquialisms and contractions as historically grounded; judge current colloquial use in light of these precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhymes and meter in older poetry provide evidence for historical pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent rhymes or imperfect rhymes in older poetry reflect historical pronunciations; such rhymes are evidence for how words were once sounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous cited rhymes (e.g., Dryden rhyming 'blown' with 'towns', Donne rhyming 'again' with 'sin', Chapman rhyming 'verse' and 'pierce') are used to infer past pronunciations. When assessing a dialectal form, consult poetic rhymes as phonological evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation differences alone are not proof of vulgarity if attested historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronunciation differences (elisions, vowels, stress) should not be deemed vulgar merely because they differ from contemporary 'polite' usage if historical or literary attestations exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly shows many 'Yankee' pronunciations mirrored in respected earlier writers; use historical attestation to rebut claims of vulgarity. Examples: 'shet' (shut), 'risse'/'rize' (rose), 'wex' (wax), etc.
